body: Wednesday, June 24 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed held rates at its June 17 meeting, removing its prior cutting bias and signaling potential hikes ahead under new Chair Kevin Warsh. Inflation hit a 3-year high, and the dot plot has been reshaped toward tightening. The 10Y yield at 4.41% has actually fallen 8 bps over 4 weeks — a curve-flattening signal as the 2Y at 4.16% (prior close, +3 bps vs 4W) has edged higher, compressing the spread. VIX elevated at 18.84 (+10.8% over 4W). The dollar is near 13-month highs.

New / Most Important: This is structurally the most important shift in the global macro landscape. Kevin Warsh's Fed has pivoted from a Powell-era dovish framework to an explicit hawkish hold with upside rate risk — the first time since 2018 that a Fed chair has actively telegraphed hikes as the next move. This happened against a backdrop of inflation re-acceleration, not a demand overheating but a supply-side shock from geopolitical factors (Iran deal uncertainty, tariffs). The market is repricing the entire forward curve: the "Greenspan put" debate in the WSJ signals that investors are questioning whether any equity backstop exists. JPMorgan's bullish equity call paired with flash-crash warnings captures the cognitive dissonance perfectly. FedEx returning $800M in tariff refunds hints at a trade-policy softening that hasn't fully registered. The combination of a hawkish Fed + strong dollar + crashing oil (-24.9% in 4W) creates a deeply unusual macro cocktail that compresses EM and commodity currencies while paradoxically easing imported inflation — meaning Warsh may get cover to delay actual hikes even as he talks tough.

Playbook ✓: Hawkish Fed → strong dollar → tech sells off → small caps outperform (Russell +2.9% vs Nasdaq -2.5%) — textbook rate-sensitivity rotation.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The 10Y yield is FALLING despite hawkish rhetoric — the long end is pricing in growth risk, not inflation passthrough. The 10Y-2Y spread at +34 bps at the prior close, 9 bps flatter than four weeks ago, with a falling 10Y and a firmer 2Y is a flattening pattern historically associated with policy error risk. Markets are saying Warsh may overtighten into a slowdown.

Macro Stance: The ECB faces a "mid-sized inflation shock" per Chief Economist Lane, with the central bank signaling it is ready to raise rates again but not immediately. EUR/USD has fallen to a one-year low. The collapse in oil prices (-24.9%) eases imported energy inflation and reduces pressure on the ECB to hike — but core inflation remains sticky.

New / Most Important: The euro's rout to one-year lows is a capital flow story, not just a rate differential story. The Nikkei Shimbun piece on Japanese investors pouring into US stocks, and the Forbes headline on $14 trillion of foreign buying adding to US equity values, suggest Europe is on the wrong side of a gravitational capital flow. The ECB's hike — which was supposed to provide yield support for EUR — has instead become a growth headwind, per EBC Financial Group's analysis. This is a classic trap: hiking into weakness while capital exits toward the US. The ECB assessing euro adoption in five EU countries signals institutional concern about the currency bloc's cohesion under stress.

Playbook ✓: Strong dollar + ECB hawkishness = EUR weakness — standard divergence trade.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Oil crashing should be a massive terms-of-trade positive for Europe, yet the euro is falling anyway. This means capital outflows are overwhelming the energy windfall — a structural bearish signal for European assets that contradicts the typical energy-importer playbook.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is easing through plumbing, not price. Loan prime rates stayed unchanged for a 13th month (Reuters, [Jun 21]), but at the Lujiazui Forum the central bank hinted at a shift towards an overnight policy rate to match global peers (The Business Times, [Jun 17]); Capital Economics expects a narrower rate corridor but sees no signs of healthier credit ([Jun 19]). The yuan is the release valve: the fixing was weakened for a fourth session as the dollar advanced (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]), even as Germany's Merz seeks currency talks to fix an undervalued yuan (Bloomberg, [Jun 19]) and Lagarde urges talks on its undervaluation (SCMP, [Jun 23]). Prices split: May CPI rose 1.2% (China Daily, [Jun 10]), an unexpected stall despite the oil shock (Bloomberg, [Jun 9]), while factory-gate inflation hit a nearly four-year high (Reuters, [Jun 9]).

PMIs & Activity: May's official manufacturing PMI dropped to 50 (Xinhua, [May 31]) as factory activity stalled on weaker demand (Reuters, [May 30]); non-manufacturing rose to 50.1 (Macau Business, [May 31]). The private gauge slowed but still showed factory activity expanding for a sixth month (Reuters, [May 31]). The hard data diverge: industrial output growth quickened while retail sales and investment contracted (Reuters, [Jun 15]); retail sales fell 0.6%, the first decline since 2022 (Il Sole 24 ORE, [Jun 15]), and fixed-asset investment was down 4.1% in the first five months (Macau Business, [Jun 16]). Exports jumped 19.4% (AP News, [Jun 9]). June has not turned: the 618 festival saw flat e-commerce sales (Reuters, [Jun 22]).

Credit Impulse: May credit growth topped forecasts in a rebound from the lending slump (Bloomberg, [Jun 12]), yet new loans missed as the property slump curbed demand (Reuters, [Jun 12]) and households kept deleveraging (SCMP, [Jun 15]). The two reconcile through the mix: the beat came from outside bank loans, in line with the tilt to bonds from loans (Bloomberg, [Jun 17]), and the PBOC chief says slower credit growth may be the "new normal" (Caixin, [Jun 18]). The private impulse is impaired: a 2.2 trillion yuan pile of bad consumer debt threatens the economy (The Business Times, [Jun 18]).

Property: May new home prices fell at a faster pace on soft demand (Reuters, [Jun 15]), even as first-tier new home prices rose for a third month (SCMP, [Jun 16]) and top cities extended a secondhand-home price rebound (Caixin, [Jun 17]). Construction is the drag: property investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May (GMK Center, [Jun 18]) and the steel market has entered a long plateau after the property crash (Bloomberg, [Jun 21]). Policies delivered an uptick in property sales (The Star, [Jun 19]), but developer stress persists: Oaktree and PAG are vying with Arkkan over a Chinese builder's debt plan (Bloomberg, [Jun 17]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The fiscal stance is tightening into the slowdown: China pursued austerity with its first fiscal-gap cutback since 2023 (Bloomberg, [Jun 22]), the deficit narrowing for the first time in over two years despite slowing growth (Firstpost, [Jun 23]). Support is targeted instead: Beijing readies a fresh $9 billion consumer stimulus as retail sales shrink (Caixin, [Jun 18]) and CNY 200 billion of "Two New" funds to be fully deployed by end-June (BigGo Finance, [Jun 17]). On trade, Beijing added 10 US firms, including a rare-earth miner, to its export control list (Al Jazeera, [Jun 22]) and hit Australian beef with a 55% tariff once the quota was reached (Nikkei Asia, [Jun 19]). The EU is reportedly preparing tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrids (Reuters, [Jun 19]); its trade chief is set to host China's commerce minister (Reuters, [Jun 22]).

Markets & Flows: Hong Kong prices the consumer slump. The Hang Seng hit its lowest level in a year on rate-rise expectations (SCMP, [Jun 18]) and then plunged 432 points through 23,300 as the HSCEI entered a technical bear market (BigGo Finance, [Jun 23]), a slide Bloomberg ties to spending woes ([Jun 23]). AI is the exception: Chinese AI stocks rallied on demand optimism and policy support (Bloomberg, [Jun 21]). Flows favour new supply: a Hynix ETF has toppled the Hong Kong Tracker Fund with $17 billion of assets (Bloomberg, [Jun 22]), echoing SK Hynix's $29B ADR plan, and China Resources New Energy drew 6.4 trillion yuan in retail bids for the biggest Shenzhen IPO (The Business Times, [Jun 23]).

New / Most Important: Beijing is tightening fiscal policy into a domestic-demand slump. The first deficit cutback since 2023 follows the first fall in retail sales in over three years, and the response stays targeted: a $9 billion consumer package, funds already in the pipeline and a hinted shift to an overnight policy rate, not a demand stimulus. Markets have answered: the HSCEI is in a technical bear market on spending woes, and the yuan fixing has been weakened for a fourth session, a release valve Berlin and the ECB now openly contest.

Playbook ✓: Weak consumption, falling home prices and booming exports met by unchanged LPRs and targeted support are on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Policy leans on supply and the currency rather than demand: austerity, a weaker fixing and 19.4% export growth push excess output abroad. European exporters are squeezed: BMW's profit warning highlights China risk (Reuters, [Jun 17]), while plug-in hybrid tariffs and the yuan dispute raise trade-war risk for EU autos. Construction commodities lose: iron ore has sunk back below $100 on abundant supplies (Bloomberg, [Jun 17]) and property investment down 16.2% offers no demand offset, leaving the AUD exposed, with a 55% beef tariff on top. For oil, the China channel runs through Iran: Kpler expects Iranian oil to flow mainly to China despite the 60-day sanctions waiver ([Jun 23]), so the waiver frees few barrels for other buyers. EM fixed income wins, as Pimco sees China's export glut boosting emerging-market bonds (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]).

Macro Stance: The BOJ raised rates to 1% — the highest since 1995 — and Governor Ueda signaled more hikes ahead. Inflation may exceed the 2% target. Despite $70B+ in FX intervention and rate hikes, the yen remains near intervention zones around 161.60 per dollar. Some BOJ members called for even faster hikes.

New / Most Important: This is a structurally unprecedented situation. Japan has rates at 1%, the highest in three decades, and is actively intervening in FX markets, yet the yen continues to weaken. The carry trade — which the June 2024 BOJ hike was supposed to unwind — has reconstituted itself because the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot widened the US-Japan rate differential further. Japanese retail and institutional investors are simultaneously buying US stocks (Nikkei Shimbun/Milhaupt reporting), creating a self-reinforcing capital outflow that undermines intervention. The ex-BOJ policymaker warning that a Fed hike could push USDJPY to 165 tells you the BOJ has lost control of the currency through rates alone. Japan's equity market is rotating from value to growth on the AI boom, meaning domestic equity flows aren't providing yen support either. This is a carry trade on steroids: the more Japan hikes, the more it slows domestic growth without narrowing the rate gap enough to matter, because the Fed keeps moving the goalposts. The intervention risk creates two-way volatility but not trend reversal.

Playbook ✓: BOJ hawkishness → Nikkei selloff (down 0.71%) — rate-sensitive equities repricing.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The yen carry trade surviving a 1% policy rate and massive intervention is a structural break from all historical precedent. Capital flows are overwhelming monetary policy.

Macro Stance: The RBA held rates at its recent meeting, but Deputy Governor Hauser stated inflation "remains far too high." Headline CPI cooled but core CPI remains sticky, keeping rate hike bets alive. Bond traders won't rule out a fourth rate rise.

New / Most Important: Australia sits in the worst possible macro position for a commodity-linked economy: oil is down 24.9% and China is weakening — China's May retail sales fell for the first time in over three years, its property investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May and Beijing has hit Australian beef with a 55% tariff — yet domestic inflation is sticky enough that hikes remain on the table. The AUD is being supported only by lingering rate hike expectations — the China-demand cushion is gone.  |  Playbook ✓: Sticky core inflation + hawkish RBA rhetoric = AUD resilience despite commodity weakness.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The collapsing commodity complex should be disinflationary, but Australian core CPI isn't responding — suggesting domestic services inflation is entrenched, a structural problem that rate hikes alone may not solve.

Macro Stance: The NBP remains in a holding pattern, but the Council is less dovish than disinflation implies: the NBP's voting record showed who backed a hike (Tysol.pl, [Jun 22]) and Gazeta Prawna headlined Iwona Duda's comments "no quick RPP decisions?" ([Jun 17]), while the Czech National Bank hiked next door (ING Think, [Jun 18]). Inflation drew level with the EU average (Business Insider Polska, [Jun 17]) and food cost only 2.4% more than a year earlier (Forsal.pl, [Jun 22]), but producer prices are rising again after almost two years of deflation (CEO Magazyn, [Jun 22]). Activity is two-speed. May industrial output rose 4.1% y/y, above consensus (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 19]), and new orders jumped more than 140% on what experts call a "SAFE effect" (Interia Biznes, [Jun 24]). Retail sales missed again, "2026 will not be the year of the consumer" (wnp.pl, [Jun 22]), and construction slowed despite EU billions (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 22]). Enterprise wages rose 5.8% y/y, below expectations (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 22]), fell month on month on one-off factors (TVN24, [Jun 22]) and employment fell (CEO Magazyn, [Jun 22]), though pay still outpaces prices (XYZ, [Jun 22]).

Markets: The Fed's hawkish hold set the tone: the WIG turned back from its bull-market peak (Bankier.pl, [Jun 18]) and, after a symbolic triple-witching gain (Parkiet, [Jun 19]), the slide resumed, with KGHM -6.4% against a 1.7% WIG20 drop as the dollar climbed (Bankier.pl, [Jun 23]). Wednesday was the heaviest session: WIG20 closed down 2.49% (BIZNES24, [Jun 24]), with KGHM -6.9%, Orlen -4.9%, PGE -4.6% and Allegro -4.2% (Bankier.pl, [Jun 24]) and the banks joining the drag (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 24]). Part of KGHM's move is mechanical, as Tuesday was the last day to qualify for its dividend (Strefa Inwestorów, [Jun 23]). At Tuesday's close: KGHM 349.7 (-9.0% 1W, +2.4% 4W), Orlen 129.04 (-6.8% / -9.9%), PGE 9.73 (-1.9% / -7.6%), PKO 104.4 (-1.4% / -0.6%), Pekao 231.0 (-0.7% / -5.6%), Dino 29.1 (-1.4% / -8.7%), LPP 18,480 (-2.4% / -17.8%); only Allegro 38.95 (+3.8% / +12.7%) and CD Projekt 228.7 (+2.6% / -10.6%) rose on the week. EPOL 38.73 is -3.0% 1W and -3.1% 4W. The zloty weakened for a fifth straight day with EUR/PLN above 4.28 (wnp.pl, [Jun 23]) and the dollar was the most expensive in over a year (Comparic.pl, [Jun 24]). Tuesday's close had USD/PLN at 3.7343 (+1.9% 1W, +2.8% 4W) but EUR/PLN 4.2667 only +0.4% / +0.9%: mostly a dollar move. No POLGB yield headlines this week.

Fiscal & Politics: Ministry of Finance data showed debt up 46.8 billion zloty in one month (Gazeta Prawna, Interia Biznes, [Jun 22]); NIK flagged "operations disturbing transparency" in state finances (Money.pl, [Jun 17]), the Fiscal Council warned that delaying cuts could cost Poland dearly (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 17]) and Zero.pl reports tax rises in preparation ([Jun 19]). The first answer is a levy: the Sejm passed a 60% windfall tax on fuel companies (TVP Info, Money.pl, [Jun 19]), applying from August (GazetaPrawna.pl, [Jun 19]) and adopted within 48 hours (wPolityce.pl, [Jun 18]); the government counts on 4 billion zloty (Money.pl, [Jun 22]). Tusk told rivals that hostility toward Germany and Ukraine serves Russia (Anadolu, [Jun 17]).

Corporate & Sectors: Energy: Orlen suspended its membership of the industry body POPiHN over the levy (Interia Biznes, [Jun 22]), and wPolityce.pl tallies about 20 billion zloty of value lost in days ([Jun 22]). Orlen booked FSRU 2 capacity, taking LNG import capability above 16 billion cubic metres a year (Bankier.pl, [Jun 23]), while PGE, Enea and Unimot want gas without Orlen (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 23]) and PGE signed a regasification deal worth about 2.8 billion zloty (WysokieNapiecie.pl, [Jun 23]); a key agreement for an SMR in Włocławek was signed (TVP Bydgoszcz, [Jun 22]). Mining: KGHM's Pomeranian project gained MON backing (Bankier.pl, [Jun 23]), yet INNPoland says the share price is "bleeding" ([Jun 23]). Banks: a Supreme Court resolution on exchange-rate clauses hands CHF borrowers a new argument (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 24]); a draft gives banks nine months to offer borrowers a WIBOR switch (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 23]); investment loans are growing at a double-digit pace (pb.pl, [Jun 23]). Retail: Dino is under National Prosecutor's Office scrutiny (Bankier.pl, [Jun 18]) and LPP drew a negative recommendation (Comparic.pl, [Jun 17]). Gaming: CD Projekt is renaming itself CD Projekt RED and pays no dividend for 2025 (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 23]).

Geopolitics & Security: Latvia warned of Russian missile and drone provocations targeting the Baltics and Poland (Kyiv Post, [Jun 23]), though not of imminent full-scale war (Meduza, [Jun 23]), and Frontex flags a pressured eastern border (InfoSecurity24, [Jun 23]). Defence money is supportive: an EU military Schengen could bring Poland billions of euros (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 23]) and a permanent US base is closer, with construction due this year (TOK FM, [Jun 18]). Relations with Kyiv soured: world media warned of a crisis after a decision by President Nawrocki (GazetaPrawna.pl, [Jun 20]) and Poles launched a citizen award for Zelensky after a state honour was revoked (TVP World, [Jun 21]).

New / Most Important: The 60% windfall tax matters most because the week's two stories meet in it. A hawkish Fed and the strongest dollar in over a year explain the direction of Polish assets; the fiscal backdrop explains the thin cushion. With debt up 46.8 billion zloty in a month and both NIK and the Fiscal Council critical, the state has shown it will tap listed champions' profits and legislate in 48 hours. Orlen's -6.8% week is the first cost; the larger one is a policy-risk premium on every state-controlled WIG20 heavyweight.

Playbook ✓: Hawkish Fed → strongest dollar in over a year → zloty slide and a commodity-led blue-chip sell-off is the textbook EM response; strong dollar and EUR weakness remain headwinds for PLN.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The data do not justify the de-rating: output beat and orders surged. EUR/PLN +0.4% on the week against +1.9% for USD/PLN says the zloty is a passenger in the dollar regime, not pricing a Polish premium; equities are, with EPOL -3.0% in a week and Orlen -9.9% over four weeks reflecting fiscal and levy risk that FX has yet to price.

Macro Stance: The Indian rupee held steady as a firm US dollar was offset by lower oil prices — a natural hedge for India as a major crude importer.  |  New / Most Important: Oil's 24.9% crash in 4 weeks is the single best macro tailwind India has received in years; it directly compresses the current account deficit and eases RBI's inflation calculus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None — this is textbook India macro benefiting from an oil supply shock.
Narrative: The Nasdaq 100 is down 2.5% over 4W after a sharp 3% single-session drop, as investors pause the AI run-up and the Warsh Fed's hawkish shift pressures duration-heavy growth.

Reported: Accenture tumbled 16% on a guidance cut (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 18]) even though its Q3 earnings beat estimates on growth in managed services (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 18]); IT services stocks fell after the guidance cut, with Capgemini down 8% (Investing.com, [Jun 18]). Jabil shares rallied as earnings and revenue topped expectations (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 17]); its Q3 beat came on AI infrastructure strength (Zacks Investment Research, [Jun 18]).
EPS Upside Watch: Fortinet — getting a network-firewall boost from AI data centres, a picks-and-shovels play that gains from the build-out more reliably than the GPU makers.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The market is differentiating within AI rather than buying a monolith: it pays the builders (Jabil) and sells IT services, where weak demand is a key concern and AI alone is not to blame (Moneycontrol.com, [Jun 19]) — the shift from "rising tide" to a stock picker's market.

Narrative: Communications is caught in the broader tech sell-off but less exposed to the semiconductor and AI-hardware repricing, and GTA 6 dominating social feeds is a consumer-engagement signal for Take-Two and interactive media.
Reported: Tech investor Prosus posted a core earnings rise on growth across its units and Tencent (WSJ, [Jun 19]).

EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet — Wall Street keeps raising its target while the stock slips (TIKR.com, [Jun 21]), so estimates are moving ahead of the price. Take-Two — the GTA 6 launch is a $2B+ single-title revenue event at an affordable price point.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Banks await stress tests for major banks (Seeking Alpha, [Jun 19]), historically a buyback catalyst; a firm 2Y (4.16% at the prior close, +3 bps vs 4W) supports asset yields, and BofA and Deutsche Bank expect the Fed to raise rates in September (Reuters, [Jun 22]), though the flat +34 bps 10Y-2Y spread limits margin expansion.
Reported: Standard Bank maintained its guidance despite an uncertain operating environment (Business Day, [Jun 22]), shrugging off global uncertainty with steady growth (Moneyweb, [Jun 22]).

EPS Upside Watch: Standard Chartered — upgraded by Deutsche Bank as the Asian wealth boom drives its earnings outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]). JPMorgan — a clean stress-test pass would unlock larger capital returns through buybacks and dividends.

⚡ Breaking Convention: JPMorgan is bullish on equities while warning of a flash crash brewing in crowded trades — staying long while hedging the tail. When the largest bank on the street talks about crowding risk, the unwind catalyst is usually closer than the median forecast assumes.
Narrative: WTI has collapsed 24.9% in 4 weeks to $70.54 as Iran peace-talk progress strips out the geopolitical risk premium, and the strong dollar adds pressure.
Reported: Karoon Energy cut its CY26 guidance as Who Dat slipped to 2H27 (Stocks Down Under, [Jun 17]).

EPS Upside Watch: BPCL and IOC — JP Morgan says falling crude prices will boost oil marketing companies' margins, with the two likely to benefit most (The New Indian Express, [Jun 22]): cheaper crude widens the downstream spread.

⚡ Breaking Convention: A 25% oil crash should be inflation relief that lets central banks ease, yet the Fed, ECB, BOJ and RBA are all holding or hiking — the oil deflation impulse is being ignored. Energy equities already price lower oil; the real question is whether E&Ps cut capex, which would set up the next supply squeeze in 12-18 months.

Narrative: US manufacturing activity hit a 4-year high in June (Firstpost, [Jun 23]), FedEx's $800M tariff-refund return signals trade-policy softening, and small-cap outperformance (Russell +2.9%) favours domestic industrials.

Reported: Bunzl upgraded its outlook and topped the FTSE 100 (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]). FirstGroup beat forecasts with its FY profits and announced a £100m buyback (Sharecast.com, [Jun 18]). Primoris Services sank after a guidance cut as renewables overruns deepened (Quiver Quantitative, [Jun 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: Southwest Airlines — UBS raised its price target to $61 on the earnings outlook (Investing.com, [Jun 23]), with WTI down 24.9% in four weeks cutting the fuel bill.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Output is at a 4-year high while US factory job cuts are the worst since 2009 (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 23]): the manufacturing upturn is margin-led, not hiring-led — good for industrial EPS, but a weaker labour signal than the activity data suggest.

Narrative: Lower gas prices from the oil crash are a direct consumer tailwind and GTA 6 engagement shows discretionary spend is alive, but margins and credit, not demand, are the pressure point in the results.

Reported: CarMax dropped 7% despite an earnings beat and Carvana tumbled 8% on used-car margin and credit fears (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 17]). Carnival shares fell as its Q3 outlook missed estimates despite an earnings beat (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 23]). UK retailer AO World logged a record profit as discounts and membership drew shoppers (Reuters, [Jun 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: CAVA — its pullback triggered a "historically bullish signal", and TIKR's $213 target implies around 139% total return (TIKR.com, [Jun 20]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail stocks tumbled despite strong earnings (MoneySense, [Jun 18]): with cheaper gas a known tailwind, the market treats the beat as priced and pays only for margin and guidance.
Narrative: Staples are a defensive-rotation beneficiary with the VIX elevated at 18.84, and a "shift toward quality stocks" as rates stay high supports the positioning.

Reported: Kroger's Q1 earnings miss weighed on its shares despite in-line sales (ChartMill, [Jun 18]) as comp sales underwhelmed (Grocery Dive, [Jun 18]). Alimentation Couche-Tard's profit rose on increased same-store sales (WSJ, [Jun 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: L'Oréal — Jefferies lifted its price target, though it warned of overvaluation, making it the barometer for premium consumers' willingness to pay.
⚡ Breaking Convention: Defensive is not the same as safe on results: Kroger was sold on a miss even in a tape rotating into staples, so the bid is for quality execution, not the sector label.

Narrative: The US decrying "free rides" from countries whose public health systems negotiate drug prices is headline risk for pharma with global pricing exposure — watch for executive orders on reference pricing — while the defensive sector benefits from risk-off rotation and Yardeni sees pockets of alpha inside healthcare (Yardeni QuickTakes, [Jun 21]).
Reported: No major reports this week.
EPS Upside Watch: Dr Reddy's — Nomura sees 35% upside potential after its strategic consumer health pivot (The Financial Express, [Jun 23]), a mix shift toward consumer health.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Copper at $5.95 (-6.5% 4W), the AI data-centre and grid metal, and gold at $4,024 (-10.6% 4W) are both falling as a hawkish Fed and a dollar near 13-month highs pull liquidity from the whole commodity complex.

Reported: Alamos Gold shares plunged on an output cut after an earthquake at its mine (Bloomberg, [Jun 19]). Satellite Chemical hit its daily limit up after forecasting first-half net profit to surge over 118% to a record, as its ethane-based route crushes oil-based rivals on cost (BigGo Finance, [Jun 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: PETRONAS Chemicals — Maybank expects its earnings to rise in 2Q, though not sustainably as prices retreat (The Edge Malaysia, [Jun 23]). Newmont — a top pick as gold's pullback looks temporary (Market Index, [Jun 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold falling 10.6% in 4 weeks with the VIX elevated at 18.84 breaks the risk-off playbook: Warsh's hawkish Fed is pushing real rates higher and the dollar to 13-month highs, overwhelming safe-haven demand. Gold is trading as a duration asset, not a hedge — a regime change for portfolio construction.

Narrative: The "Housing Bill" trending alongside Speaker Johnson signals legislative action, but 30-year mortgage rates climbed to 6.61% (WSJ, [Jun 23]) and US housing starts fell to the lowest level since 2020 (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 19]); REITs face the hawkish-Fed headwind directly.

Reported: KB Home beat Q2 sales expectations (StockStory, [Jun 23]) and its Q2 earnings met estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 23]), but it reported lower revenue as the difficult housing market persists (WSJ, [Jun 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Realty Income — a highest-conviction call points to 30% upside (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 18]); the net-lease landlord gains most if the 10Y keeps easing from 4.41% (-8 bps over 4W).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Cheaper oil should be housing's relief valve, yet mortgage rates tick higher as traders price in a Fed hike (HousingWire, [Jun 23]): the front end, not energy, sets the cost of a home loan, so the bill's supply measures matter more than the oil crash.

Narrative: Utilities are a defensive haven with the VIX elevated and the 10Y down 8 bps over 4W to 4.41%; AI data-centre power demand remains the structural tailwind, and solar is being called a buy-the-dip.
Reported: UK multi-utility Telecom Plus shares tanked 25% on its profit outlook and a dividend cut (Sharecast.com, [Jun 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Dominion Energy — the world's largest data-centre utility has a $93 target (TIKR.com, [Jun 19]), with data-centre load as the earnings driver.
